questions.question: How do you reverse a singly linked list in Java? Implement both iterative and recursive approaches and walk through the pointer mechanics.
questions.title: Reverse a Linked List — Iterative and Recursive in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Iterative approach (preferred)**: use three pointers — `prev`, `curr`, `next` — and reverse one link at a time. Start with `prev = null, curr = head`; at each step save `next = curr.next`, flip `curr.next = prev`, then advance `prev = curr; curr = next`. When `curr == null`, `prev` is the new head. **Time O(n), Space O(1)**. **Recursive approach**: recursively reverse the rest of the list (`newHead = reverse(head.next)`), then flip the current node's pointers (`head.next.next = head; head.next = null`). **Time O(n), Space O(n) for recursion stack**. For interviews, always **start with iterative** because it's O(1) space and more production-safe (no stack overflow on large lists). Use recursive if specifically asked or for elegance. **Both must handle edge cases**: empty list (`head == null` → return null), single node (`head.next == null` → return head). **Common variants**: reverse a sublist `[m, n]` (add dummy head; reverse the middle segment; reconnect); reverse in groups of K (iteratively reverse each K-block; harder); reverse a doubly-linked list (swap prev/next at each node — simpler than singly). **Common bugs**: losing the rest of the list (must save `next` before flipping); forgetting to null out the new tail's `.next` in recursion (would create a cycle); not returning the new head. For **Java 21+** streaming contexts, avoid `Collectors.toList()` reversal tricks; stick to classical pointer manipulation. **Stack-safe recursion** via explicit iteration is always the right production choice.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Losing track of the next node (forgetting to save `curr.next` before flipping). Forgetting to set the new tail's `.next = null` in recursion. Not handling empty / single-node cases

sections.title: Iterative Reversal — O(1) Space
sections.content:
```java
public ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;
    ListNode curr = head;
    while (curr != null) {
        ListNode next = curr.next;   // save next before losing it
        curr.next = prev;             // flip the link
        prev = curr;                  // advance prev
        curr = next;                  // advance curr
    }
    return prev;   // prev is the new head (last original node)
}
```

**Walkthrough** on `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null`:

Initial: `prev=null, curr=1`.

**Iter 1**: next=2; 1.next=null; prev=1; curr=2. List so far: `null <- 1 , 2 -> 3`.

**Iter 2**: next=3; 2.next=1; prev=2; curr=3. List: `null <- 1 <- 2 , 3`.

**Iter 3**: next=null; 3.next=2; prev=3; curr=null. List: `null <- 1 <- 2 <- 3`.

Return prev=3. New head is 3.

**Time**: O(n) — single pass.
**Space**: O(1) — just three pointer variables.

**Why this is the preferred production answer**:
- No recursion stack risk for long lists.
- Simple, visual with a diagram.
- Easy to adapt for variants (reverse sublist, K-group reversal).

**Edge cases**:
- `head == null` → loop doesn't execute; return prev = null.
- Single node → next=null; 1.next=null (no-op); prev=1; curr=null. Return 1.
- Two nodes `1 -> 2` → correctly reversed to `2 -> 1`.

sections.title: Recursive Reversal — O(n) Stack
sections.content:
```java
public ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    if (head == null || head.next == null) return head;
    ListNode newHead = reverseList(head.next);   // recursively reverse rest
    head.next.next = head;                        // make next node point back to head
    head.next = null;                             // current head becomes new tail
    return newHead;
}
```

**How it works** on `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null`:

1. reverseList(1): not base case; recurse on reverseList(2).
2. reverseList(2): not base case; recurse on reverseList(3).
3. reverseList(3): base case (head.next == null); return 3.
4. Back in reverseList(2): newHead=3; head=2, head.next=3. We do 3.next = 2, 2.next = null. Now 2 <- 3, and 2 is tail. Return newHead=3.
5. Back in reverseList(1): newHead=3; head=1, head.next=2. We do 2.next = 1, 1.next = null. Now 1 <- 2 <- 3, and 1 is tail. Return newHead=3.

**Final list**: `3 -> 2 -> 1 -> null`.

**The key line**: `head.next.next = head;` means 'make the node after head point back to head'. And `head.next = null;` makes the current head the new tail.

**Time**: O(n).
**Space**: O(n) — recursion stack, one frame per node.

**Stack overflow risk**: Java's default stack is ~10K frames. `reverseList(10000)` throws StackOverflowError. For long lists, use iterative or increase stack (`-Xss16m`).

**When to use recursive**: if asked specifically, for elegance, or when the list is bounded and short. Otherwise iterative is strictly better in production.

sections.title: Edge Cases and Common Bugs
sections.content:
**Edge cases**:
- **Empty list (`head == null`)**: return null.
- **Single node**: return head unchanged.
- **Two nodes**: ensure correct flip.
- **All identical values**: algorithm unaffected; just reverses references.

**Common bugs**:

**1. Losing the rest of the list**
- Forgetting to save `curr.next` before flipping.
- Symptom: NPE or truncated list.
- Fix: always save `next = curr.next` first.

**2. Creating a cycle (recursive)**
- Forgetting `head.next = null` after the recursive flip.
- Symptom: infinite loop when traversing the reversed list.
- Fix: always set `head.next = null` for the old head (new tail).

**3. Not returning the new head**
- Iterative: returning `head` (now at null) instead of `prev`.
- Recursive: returning `head` instead of `newHead`.

**4. Off-by-one in sublist reversal**
- Iterating wrong number of times.
- Off-by-one in preStart advancement (should advance m-1 times to reach node before m).

**5. Stack overflow for long lists**
- Recursive version throws StackOverflowError.
- Fix: use iterative.

**6. Modifying the wrong pointer**
- `curr.next = prev` vs `prev.next = curr` — subtle but critical.
- Drawing a diagram prevents this.

**Best practice**: always **draw the list** with pointers before coding. Label `prev`, `curr`, `next`. Simulate one or two iterations by hand. This catches 90% of bugs before compilation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Iterative reversal**: three pointers (`prev`, `curr`, `next`), O(n) time, **O(1) space**.
- **Core steps**: save next, flip link, advance.
- **Recursive reversal**: reverse rest, connect back, null old next. O(n) time, **O(n) space** (stack).
- **Iterative is preferred** for production: no stack overflow, simpler for variants.
- **Use dummy head** for sublist reversal to uniformly handle edge cases.
- **Reverse K-group**: iterate blocks; within each, reverse using iterative method; thread blocks together.
- **Edge cases**: empty list, single node.
- **Common bugs**: losing rest (forget next), cycle in recursion (forget null), wrong return value.
- **Draw the list** before coding to catch pointer errors.
- **Stack overflow**: recursive fails on long lists (~10K nodes default).
- **Doubly-linked list**: swap prev/next at each node — even simpler.
- **Related problems**: palindrome check (reverse second half), add two numbers (reverse, add, reverse), merge sort (reverse split for comparison).
- **O(1) space** is the headline advantage of iterative.
- **Always return the new head** — not the old head (which is now the tail).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Iterative reversal — the standard approach**

**Three pointers**: prev, curr, next
- Start: prev = null, curr = head
- Each iteration:
  - Save next = curr.next (don't lose the rest)
  - Flip: curr.next = prev
  - Advance: prev = curr; curr = next
- When curr is null: return prev (new head)

**Time O(n), Space O(1)**

**Why iterative is preferred**
- O(1) space (just three pointers)
- No stack overflow risk
- Easy to adapt for variants
- Production-safe for any list size

**Walkthrough on 1 → 2 → 3**

**Iter 1**: next=2, 1.next=null, prev=1, curr=2. List: null ← 1, 2 → 3.

**Iter 2**: next=3, 2.next=1, prev=2, curr=3. List: null ← 1 ← 2, 3.

**Iter 3**: next=null, 3.next=2, prev=3, curr=null. List: null ← 1 ← 2 ← 3.

Return prev=3.

**Recursive reversal**

- Base case: head == null or head.next == null → return head
- Recursive: newHead = reverse(head.next)
- Flip: head.next.next = head; head.next = null
- Return newHead

**How it works**
- Recursion reaches the tail, which becomes the new head
- Unwinding: each node flips its `.next.next` to itself, then nulls its own `.next`
- Keeps passing the same newHead up

**Time O(n), Space O(n)** — stack frames

**Stack overflow risk**
- Default Java stack ~10K frames
- reverse(10000) throws StackOverflowError
- Use iterative for long lists

**Edge cases**
- Empty: head == null → return null
- Single node: return head
- Two nodes: correctly reversed

**Reverse sublist [m, n]**
- Use dummy head to uniformly handle m=1
- Advance to node before m (preStart)
- Reverse the segment (standard iterative)
- Reconnect: preStart.next.next = segment.tail.next; preStart.next = new segment head
- O(n) time, O(1) space

**Reverse K-group**
- Iterate, take groups of K
- Reverse each group
- Thread back together with dummy head
- If fewer than K remain, leave as-is
- O(n) time, O(1) space

**Doubly-linked list reversal**
- Swap prev/next at each node
- Then the old tail becomes new head
- Simpler than singly-linked (both pointers always set)

**Common bugs**

**1. Losing the rest of the list**
- Forgetting to save next before flipping
- Always: next = curr.next FIRST

**2. Creating a cycle (recursive)**
- Forgetting head.next = null
- Traversing the reversed list loops forever

**3. Not returning new head**
- Return prev (iterative) or newHead (recursive)
- Not head (now at null or tail)

**4. Off-by-one in sublist version**
- Advance preStart m-1 times (to node before m)
- Not m times

**5. Modifying wrong pointer**
- curr.next = prev (flip current node's link)
- Not prev.next = curr
- Draw a diagram if unsure

**Related problems**

**Palindrome linked list**
- Find middle (slow/fast)
- Reverse second half
- Compare first half and reversed second half
- O(n) time, O(1) space

**Add two numbers (lists)**
- If stored least-significant-digit-first: just iterate
- If most-significant-first: reverse, add, reverse (or use stack)

**Swap pairs / reverse in pairs**
- Special case of K-group with K=2

**Iterative recipe to remember**
1. prev=null, curr=head
2. while curr != null:
   - next = curr.next
   - curr.next = prev
   - prev = curr
   - curr = next
3. return prev

**Recursive recipe**
1. If head null or head.next null: return head
2. newHead = reverse(head.next)
3. head.next.next = head
4. head.next = null
5. return newHead

**Recommendation:** Always **start with the iterative approach** — it's O(1) space, has no stack-overflow risk, and extends naturally to variants (reverse sublist, K-group reversal, pair swap). Memorize the **three-pointer recipe**: save next, flip link, advance prev and curr. Draw the list with pointer labels when coding; this catches 90% of bugs before they happen. The **recursive approach** is elegant but has O(n) stack space and fails on long lists (~10K+ nodes default Java stack); mention it as an alternative when asked, but recommend iterative for production. The **three critical pointer moves** in the recursive version are: **newHead = reverse(head.next)** (recurse on the rest), **head.next.next = head** (make the next node point back to current), **head.next = null** (current becomes new tail). Forgetting the last line creates a cycle. For **variants**, use a **dummy head** to uniformly handle edge cases where the head itself changes (sublist reversal starting at m=1, K-group reversal). For **doubly-linked lists**, just swap prev/next at each node — simpler than singly-linked. Related problems like **palindrome linked list** and **Kth from end** build on these pointer-manipulation skills. The mental model: **reverse = flip each link one at a time, carefully tracking where each node points**. Once you can draw the transformation on a whiteboard, the code writes itself.

questions.question: How do you detect a loop in a linked list in Java? Implement Floyd's cycle detection, find the cycle length, and locate the cycle's start node.
questions.title: Detect a Loop in a Linked List — Floyd's Cycle Detection with Cycle Start
questions.direct_answer: **Floyd's algorithm (tortoise and hare)** uses two pointers moving at different speeds: `slow` advances one node per step; `fast` advances two. If they ever meet, there's a cycle; if `fast` hits null, there isn't. **Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space**. **Cycle length**: once they meet, fix one pointer and advance the other until they meet again; count the steps. **Cycle start**: after detection, reset one pointer to head and advance both at speed 1 — they meet at the cycle's start. The math: if L = distance from head to cycle start, C = cycle length, D = distance from cycle start to meeting point, then fast traveled 2(L+D) and slow traveled L+D; their difference equals kC (fast made k extra laps) — so L = kC - D, which means 'distance from head to start equals distance from meeting to start (mod C)'. **Alternatives**: **HashSet** (O(n) time, O(n) space) — simpler; each node tracked by reference. **Marking visited** — mutates nodes (adds a flag field), usually not allowed. **Brent's algorithm** — ~36% fewer pointer advances than Floyd's but less well-known. **Edge cases**: empty list, single node, self-loop, cycle at the very end, cycle at the very beginning. For interviews, Floyd's is the expected answer due to its O(1) space. The **HashSet variant** is acceptable if you explain the space trade-off. Don't mutate nodes unless explicitly allowed. This pattern generalizes to **any deterministic state transition** (happy number, find duplicate in array [1..n]).

sections.title: Detecting the Cycle
Finding Cycle Length
Finding Cycle Start
Edge Cases and Common Bugs
sections.content:
**Edge cases**:
- **Empty list**: return false / null.
- **Single node, no cycle**: fast.next == null immediately, return false.
- **Single node, self-loop (1 -> 1)**: slow=1, fast=1; both advance to 1 (self); `slow == fast` → true. Cycle start = 1.
- **Cycle starts at head**: L = 0; phase 2 immediately returns head.
- **Cycle of length 1 (tail points to itself)**: C = 1; detected correctly.
- **Long non-cycle prefix**: both pointers traverse it in O(prefix length) before entering cycle; still O(n) total.

**Common bugs**:

**1. NPE on fast.next.next**
- Always check `fast != null && fast.next != null` before advancing.
- Wrong: `while (fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null)` — misses the case where fast itself is null.

**2. Confusing meeting point with cycle start**
- They're different in general!
- Need phase 2 to find cycle start.

**3. Not understanding the math**
- Often asked to prove why phase 2 works.
- Memorize: L = kC - D.

**4. Incorrect initial pointers in phase 2**
- Start second pointer at head, not at slow's original position.
- Keep slow (or fast) at the meeting point.

**5. Modifying the list**
- Some solutions add a 'visited' flag to nodes, requiring mutation.
- Not safe if the list is shared or if nodes don't have a free flag field.

**Performance tips**:
- Floyd's chases pointers — cache-unfriendly. On huge lists, this is the dominant cost.
- For short lists, HashSet might actually be faster in wall-time despite O(n) space (fewer cache misses).
- JIT inlines trivial methods; keep traversal loops simple.

sections.title: Floyd's vs HashSet vs Brent's
sections.content:
**Floyd's (tortoise and hare)**
- O(n) time, **O(1) space**.
- Requires phase 2 for cycle start (extra O(n) time).
- Elegant, canonical.

**HashSet**
- O(n) time, **O(n) space**.
- Cycle start: first re-seen node (trivial).
- Simpler to code and explain.

**Brent's algorithm**
- O(n) time, O(1) space.
- ~36% fewer pointer advances than Floyd's.
- Uses teleportation: slow jumps to fast at exponentially growing intervals.
- Less well-known; usually beyond interview scope.

**When to choose**:
- **Interviews**: Floyd's is the expected answer.
- **Production, memory-constrained**: Floyd's.
- **Production, code clarity**: HashSet.
- **Competitive programming with huge lists**: consider Brent's.

**Performance in practice**:
- Cache: all three are cache-unfriendly on long linked lists.
- Wall-time for short lists: HashSet's allocation may make Floyd's faster despite extra traversals.
- Wall-time for long lists: Floyd's wins on memory, and therefore on cache.

**Never use node mutation** (adding visited flag) unless explicitly permitted. Shared lists or immutable data structures forbid it.

sections.title: Generalization — Beyond Linked Lists
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Floyd's algorithm**: slow (1 step), fast (2 steps); meet → cycle; fast hits null → no cycle.
- **Time O(n), Space O(1)**.
- **Cycle detection loop condition**: `while (fast != null && fast.next != null)` to avoid NPE.
- **Cycle length**: after meeting, fix one pointer, advance the other until meeting again; count steps.
- **Cycle start (phase 2)**: reset one pointer to head, advance both at speed 1, meet at start.
- **The math**: L = kC - D, proved from 2 × slow = fast distance.
- **Alternative: HashSet** — O(n) space, simpler, first re-seen = cycle start.
- **Alternative: Brent's** — ~36% fewer advances, less well-known.
- **Don't mutate nodes** unless explicitly allowed.
- **Edge cases**: empty, single node, self-loop, cycle at head, cycle of length 1.
- **Generalizes to**: happy number, find duplicate in [1..n], PRNG cycle detection.
- **Key idea**: any deterministic 'next' function on finite state admits Floyd's.
- **Common bugs**: NPE on fast.next.next, confusing meeting with start, not restarting from head in phase 2.
- **Performance**: pointer chasing is cache-unfriendly; all approaches have similar wall-time on long lists.
- **For interviews**: Floyd's is the expected answer; HashSet is acceptable with trade-off explanation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Floyd's algorithm (tortoise and hare)**
- slow = head, fast = head
- slow advances 1 step, fast advances 2
- If they meet: cycle detected
- If fast or fast.next is null: no cycle

**Time O(n), Space O(1)**

**Why it works**
- No cycle: fast reaches end first
- Cycle: both eventually inside; fast gains 1 step on slow per iteration
- Within C iterations (C = cycle length), gap becomes 0

**Critical null check**
- `fast != null && fast.next != null`
- Needed because we dereference fast.next.next
- Without: NPE

**Finding cycle length**
- After meeting, fix one pointer, advance the other
- Count steps until back at same position
- That count = cycle length

**Finding cycle start (phase 2)**
- After detecting cycle: reset one pointer to head
- Advance both at speed 1
- They meet at cycle start

**The math**
- L = distance head → cycle start
- C = cycle length
- D = distance cycle start → meeting point
- Slow traveled L+D; fast traveled L+D+kC
- Fast = 2 × slow: 2(L+D) = L+D+kC
- Simplify: L = kC - D
- Meaning: distance from head to start = distance from meeting to start (mod C)
- Walking both at speed 1 converges at the start

**Edge cases**
- Empty: head null → false/null
- Single node, no cycle: fast.next null, false
- Single node, self-loop: both at same node → true
- Cycle at head: L = 0, phase 2 returns head immediately
- Cycle of length 1: detected correctly

**Alternatives**

**HashSet**
- Track visited nodes by reference
- O(n) time, **O(n) space**
- First re-seen node = cycle start (trivial)
- Simpler to code
- Use when memory not critical

**Brent's algorithm**
- Teleport slow to fast at exponential intervals
- ~36% fewer pointer advances
- Less well-known
- Competitive programming

**Mutation (visited flag)**
- Add a boolean to each node
- O(n) time, O(1) extra space (per-node flag overhead)
- **Usually forbidden** (shared lists, immutable data)
- Don't use unless explicitly allowed

**Common bugs**

**1. NPE on fast.next.next**
- Must check both fast and fast.next before advancing

**2. Confusing meeting point with cycle start**
- They're different!
- Need phase 2 to find start

**3. Not understanding the math**
- Interviewers often ask to prove
- Memorize L = kC - D

**4. Wrong restart in phase 2**
- Start one pointer at head
- Keep the other at meeting point
- Not: both at meeting point

**5. Wall-time assumption**
- Pointer chasing is cache-unfriendly
- HashSet allocation may offset O(n) space cost
- Benchmark in production

**Generalization — beyond linked lists**

**Happy number**
- next(n) = sum of squares of digits
- Reaches 1 (happy) or cycles
- Apply Floyd's to integer sequence
- O(log n) per step, bounded iterations

**Find duplicate in [1..n] array of size n+1**
- Treat array as function f(i) = nums[i]
- By pigeonhole, cycle exists
- Cycle start = duplicate
- O(n) time, O(1) space
- Beats sorting (O(n log n)) and hashing (O(n) space)

**PRNG cycles**
- Pseudo-random number generators have finite state
- Cycles matter for cryptography
- Floyd's / Brent's detect them

**Key insight**
- Any deterministic 'next' function on a bounded state space — Floyd's applies
- O(1) space is the headline advantage

**For interviews**
- Floyd's is the expected answer
- HashSet is acceptable with trade-off explanation
- Don't reach for mutation unless allowed

**Recommendation:** For cycle detection in linked lists, **Floyd's algorithm** is the canonical interview answer — O(n) time, **O(1) space**. Memorize the **two-phase pattern**: (1) slow/fast meet → cycle detected; (2) reset one pointer to head, advance both at speed 1, they meet at cycle start. Be ready to **prove the math** (L = kC - D) because interviewers often ask 'why does phase 2 work?' Know how to find **cycle length** too: from the meeting point, walk the cycle once. Always check **`fast != null && fast.next != null`** before advancing to avoid NPE on `fast.next.next`. For **edge cases**, handle empty list, single node, self-loop, and cycles at the head. For **alternatives**, HashSet is acceptable (O(n) space, simpler, first-re-seen = cycle start) but Floyd's is preferred when memory matters. Don't reach for **node mutation** (adding a visited flag) unless explicitly allowed — shared or immutable data structures forbid it. The pattern **generalizes beyond linked lists**: any deterministic state transition with bounded state (happy number, find duplicate in [1..n], PRNG cycles) admits Floyd's with O(1) space. The mental model: **any sequence with a deterministic next can be cycle-detected with fast/slow, using space proportional to nothing but the two pointers themselves**. Know the algorithm cold; the math proof is the differentiator.

questions.question: How do you solve the Two Sum problem in Java? Cover the HashMap O(n) approach, the two-pointer variant for sorted input, and common variants.
questions.title: Two Sum in Java — HashMap O(n), Two-Pointer Sorted, Variants
questions.direct_answer: **Problem**: given an array of integers and a target, return indices of two numbers that sum to the target. **Unsorted array — HashMap approach (O(n) time, O(n) space)**: iterate once, for each element `x` check if `target - x` is in the map; if yes, return the pair; otherwise put `x` in the map. One pass. **Sorted array — two-pointer (O(n) time, O(1) space)**: left=0, right=n-1; if sum < target, left++; if sum > target, right--; if equal, return. **Which to use**: HashMap for arbitrary input; two-pointer if input is already sorted (saves space). **Don't sort an unsorted array** to use two-pointer unless indices in sorted order are OK — sorting costs O(n log n) and loses original indices. **Common variants**: (1) **Two Sum II (sorted)** — use two-pointer. (2) **Two Sum III (data structure)** — maintain add/find operations; use HashMap counting. (3) **Two Sum BST** — in-order traversal + two-pointer, or iterative in-order. (4) **Three Sum** — sort, outer loop, two-pointer on rest (O(n²)). (5) **Four Sum** — sort, two outer loops, two-pointer (O(n³)). (6) **Two Sum ≤ K / closest pair** — sort, two-pointer variants. (7) **Pairs with specific difference** — HashMap. (8) **Count pairs** — HashMap with frequency tracking. **Edge cases**: duplicates (e.g., target=6, nums=[3,3]), negative numbers, overflow (nums[i] + nums[j] exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE — use long), no valid pair (return empty or sentinel). **The HashMap approach is the canonical interview answer**; explain both trade-offs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the O(n) HashMap trick, when to use two-pointer, handles duplicates and edge cases, and can extend to 3-sum / 4-sum
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using nested loops (O(n²)). Not handling duplicates (e.g., target=6, nums=[3,3]). Sorting an unsorted array when original indices are required

sections.title: HashMap Approach — O(n) Time
Two-Pointer Approach — Sorted Input, O(1) Space
Variants — Three Sum, Four Sum
Two Sum III — Data Structure Design
Approaches Compared
sections.content:
| Approach | Time | Space | Input Requirement | When to Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Brute force | O(n²) | O(1) | None | Never (unless n is tiny) |
| HashMap one-pass | O(n) | O(n) | None | Default for unsorted |
| Sort + two-pointer | O(n log n) | O(1) or O(n) depending on sort | None | When you need O(1) space and can lose indices |
| Two-pointer | O(n) | O(1) | Sorted | Sorted input available |
| HashSet with counting | O(n) | O(n) | None | Counting all pairs |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HashMap one-pass**: O(n) time, O(n) space; default for unsorted input.
- **Key insight**: for each element `x`, check if `target - x` was seen; store `x` for future checks.
- **Two-pointer**: O(n) time, O(1) space; requires sorted input.
- **Monotonicity argument** justifies two-pointer: moving a pointer is safe because all skipped pairs are provably wrong.
- **Don't sort unsorted array** just to use two-pointer — O(n log n) cost and loses indices.
- **Handle duplicates correctly**: target=6 with [3,3] returns [0,1] in HashMap approach.
- **Overflow**: `target - x` with `target = Integer.MIN_VALUE` overflows; use long if necessary.
- **Three Sum**: O(n²), sort + outer loop + two-pointer, skip duplicates.
- **Four Sum**: O(n³), two outer loops.
- **K-Sum**: recursion + two-pointer at base, O(n^(K-1)).
- **Count pairs**: HashMap with frequency — O(n).
- **Two Sum III (data structure)**: HashMap counting; add O(1), find O(n).
- **Two Sum BST**: two-iterator approach — O(n) time, O(h) space.
- **Edge cases**: array < 2 elements, no valid pair, negative numbers, duplicates.
- **Integer overflow**: for large values, use `(long)a + b`.
- **For interviews**: start with HashMap; mention two-pointer for sorted input.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Standard Two Sum (unsorted)**

**HashMap one-pass — O(n) time, O(n) space**

- Iterate once
- For each element x, check if `target - x` is in the map
- If yes, return [map.get(complement), current index]
- Otherwise, put x in the map
- If no pair found, return default

**Why one pass works**
- As we iterate, the map contains all previous elements
- Current element checks backward against the map
- When complement is found, both indices are available

**Duplicates**
- target=6, nums=[3,3]: first 3 stored at index 0; second 3 finds it; return [0,1]
- Works correctly

**Overflow**
- target - nums[i] can overflow if target = Integer.MIN_VALUE
- Cast to long if large values are possible

**Sorted input — Two-pointer O(n) time, O(1) space**

- left = 0, right = n-1
- sum = nums[left] + nums[right]
- If sum < target: left++
- If sum > target: right--
- If equal: return pair

**Why monotonicity works**
- sum too small → need larger → moving right left shrinks sum (wrong direction) — move left right
- sum too large → mirror
- Each move commits to skipping pairs; the argument proves we never skip a valid one

**When to use which**

**HashMap**
- Unsorted input
- Need original indices
- O(n) space OK

**Two-pointer**
- Sorted input
- Memory-constrained
- Any valid pair (don't care about original indices)

**Don't sort just to use two-pointer**
- O(n log n) sorting cost
- Loses original indices
- HashMap's O(n) is usually better

**Variants**

**Three Sum (O(n²))**
- Sort, outer loop on first element
- Two-pointer for remaining two
- Skip duplicates at each level for distinct triplets

**Four Sum (O(n³))**
- Sort, two outer loops
- Two-pointer at base

**K-Sum generalization**
- Recursion + two-pointer at base
- O(n^(K-1))

**Count pairs**
- HashMap with frequencies
- pairs += count[target - n]
- O(n) time, O(n) space

**Pairs with difference K**
- Similar to two-sum
- For each n, check n - K and n + K in seen set

**Two Sum III (data structure)**
- add: O(1) — HashMap merge count
- find: O(n) — scan keys
- Handles duplicates: target=2a needs count[a] ≥ 2

**Two Sum BST**
- Two iterators (in-order forward, reverse in-order)
- Two-pointer logic on the iterators
- O(n) time, O(h) space
- Or: in-order flatten + two-pointer, O(n) space

**Closest pair to target**
- Sort + two-pointer
- Track smallest |sum - target|

**Edge cases**

**Array < 2 elements**
- No valid pair
- Return default / throw

**No valid pair**
- Return [-1, -1] or throw IllegalArgumentException

**Negative numbers**
- Works for both approaches
- No special handling

**Duplicates**
- HashMap handles naturally
- Two-pointer + duplicates: skip manually in K-Sum variants

**Integer overflow**
- `target - x` if `target = Integer.MIN_VALUE` and `x > 0`
- Cast to long
- Or: `if (target - x == nums[j])` replaced by careful compare

**Common pitfalls**

**1. O(n²) brute force**
- Nested loops — wastes the technique

**2. Sorting unsorted input**
- Loses indices
- O(n log n) overhead
- Use HashMap instead

**3. Forgetting duplicates**
- target=6, [3,3] must return pair
- Some implementations fail here

**4. Off-by-one in two-pointer**
- `while (left < right)` — strict less, not ≤

**5. Using the same element twice**
- HashMap stores index; current index is never in map when checked
- Ensures distinct indices

**Recommendation:** For **Two Sum** on unsorted input, always start with the **HashMap one-pass** approach — O(n) time, O(n) space, handles duplicates naturally, preserves original indices. The key insight is: **for each element, check if its complement is already in the map**. If you're given **sorted input**, prefer **two-pointer** for O(1) space; never sort an unsorted array just to use two-pointer (O(n log n) cost and loses index mapping). Always handle **duplicates** correctly — target=6 with [3, 3] must return [0, 1]. Watch for **integer overflow** when target is near `Integer.MIN_VALUE`; cast to long if necessary. For **extensions**: **Three Sum** is sort + outer loop + two-pointer (O(n²)); **Four Sum** adds another outer loop (O(n³)); **K-Sum** generalizes via recursion + two-pointer at base. For **counting all pairs**, use a HashMap with frequencies. For **Two Sum III** (data structure design), maintain a counts HashMap with O(1) add and O(n) find. For **Two Sum BST**, use two iterators (in-order forward and reverse) to achieve O(n) time, O(h) space. The mental model: **Two Sum = complement lookup**; HashMap makes it O(n), sorted input makes two-pointer O(n) with O(1) space. Once you've internalized this, all K-Sum variants and related pair-finding problems become the same template with different bookkeeping.

followup_questions: Why use HashMap over sorting + two-pointer for unsorted input?
How does the HashMap approach handle duplicates like [3, 3] with target=6?
How would you extend Two Sum to Three Sum?
How do you design a data structure with add and find operations for Two Sum?
How do you handle integer overflow in Two Sum?

questions.question: How do you implement an LRU Cache in Java? Cover the LinkedHashMap approach and the HashMap + doubly-linked-list approach.
questions.title: LRU Cache in Java — LinkedHashMap and HashMap + Doubly-Linked List
questions.direct_answer: An **LRU (Least Recently Used) cache** is a fixed-capacity cache that **evicts the least-recently-used entry** when full. Required operations — `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` — both must be **O(1)**. **Two implementations**: **(1) LinkedHashMap with access order** — simplest; override `removeEldestEntry` to evict when size exceeds capacity. Java's `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder=true` in the constructor moves each accessed entry to the tail, so the head is always the LRU. **(2) HashMap + doubly-linked list** — the 'interview' answer; demonstrates understanding of O(1) invariants. The HashMap maps keys to list nodes for O(1) access; the doubly-linked list maintains order, with head = most recent and tail = least recent (or vice versa). Operations: `get` locates node via HashMap, moves to head (O(1)); `put` either updates existing (move to head) or inserts new (remove tail if over capacity). **Why doubly-linked?** Singly-linked can't delete a middle node in O(1) (would need to find its predecessor by traversal). Doubly-linked allows `node.prev.next = node.next` in O(1). **Why sentinel head/tail?** Avoids null checks; simplifies the code. **Complexity**: both approaches are **O(1) per operation, O(capacity) space**. **Thread safety**: neither is thread-safe. For concurrent LRU: `Collections.synchronizedMap` (single lock, serializes everything) or Caffeine / Guava's `LoadingCache` (lock-striped, industry standard). **Common variants**: LFU (Least Frequently Used) — uses frequency buckets, more complex; LRU with TTL (Time To Live) — expiry on top of LRU; ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache) — balances recency and frequency. **For interviews, know both implementations**: LinkedHashMap is concise (10 lines); HashMap + DLL shows deeper understanding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the O(1) constraints, knows why doubly-linked list is needed (vs singly), can use sentinel nodes, and implements both LinkedHashMap and HashMap+DLL approaches correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using singly-linked list (can't O(1) delete a middle node). Using ArrayList (O(n) removal). Forgetting to update HashMap when evicting. Not handling edge cases (capacity 0, empty cache)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why doubly-linked is necessary for O(1), discuss sentinel node trick, mention thread-safety alternatives (Caffeine, ConcurrentLinkedHashMap), contrast with LFU, and implement both versions

sections.title: LRU Cache Requirements
sections.content:
An LRU cache is a **fixed-capacity key-value store** that maintains **access order** and evicts the **least-recently-used entry** when adding a new one and capacity is full.

**Operations (both O(1))**:
- `get(key)`: return the value if present (and mark it as most-recently-used); else return -1 or throw.
- `put(key, value)`: insert or update; if new and capacity exceeded, evict the LRU entry.

**Why O(1)?** LRU caches sit on hot paths (database buffer pools, page caches, CDN caches). Any O(log n) or O(n) cost per access is unacceptable.

**What makes LRU tricky**:
- Need fast lookup → **HashMap**.
- Need to maintain access order → **linked list** (not array; array insertion/deletion in middle is O(n)).
- Need to move elements to 'most recent' position in O(1) → **doubly-linked** (singly would require O(n) to find predecessor).

**Java offers `LinkedHashMap`** which is exactly HashMap + doubly-linked list, with built-in support for access-order via the constructor flag. That's the shortcut implementation.

**For interviews**, interviewers typically want you to:
1. Acknowledge LinkedHashMap exists.
2. Implement HashMap + DLL manually to show the algorithm.
3. Discuss thread-safety if relevant.

sections.title: LinkedHashMap Approach (Short, Idiomatic)
HashMap + Doubly-Linked List — The Interview Version
Why Doubly-Linked and Not Singly-Linked?
sections.content:
**LRU must support three operations in O(1) on the list**:
1. Add to front (new MRU) — both singly and doubly support this.
2. Remove from back (evict LRU) — singly requires O(n) to find the predecessor of tail; doubly is O(1) via `tail.prev`.
3. **Move an arbitrary node to front** (on access) — singly requires O(n) to find the predecessor of that node; doubly is O(1) via `node.prev`.

**Alternative — singly-linked with 'indirect' nodes** could work but requires additional bookkeeping (e.g., a hashmap from key to predecessor), doubling complexity for no real gain. Doubly-linked is strictly cleaner.

**Alternative — ArrayList / ArrayDeque** — insertion/deletion at arbitrary positions is O(n). Not acceptable.

**Alternative — TreeMap by timestamp** — O(log n) per op, not O(1).

**Alternative — LinkedHashSet** — works for insertion-order, but no random access to move element to end in O(1) (iteration only).

**Why sentinel nodes?**
- Without sentinels: `head` and `tail` can be null, and list operations need null checks.
- With sentinels: `head` and `tail` always exist; internal nodes always have `prev` and `next` non-null.
- Example: `removeNode(node)` becomes `node.prev.next = node.next; node.next.prev = node.prev;` — always safe.
- Without sentinels: must check if `node == head` or `node == tail` — multiple branches, bug-prone.

sections.title: Thread-Safe LRU Cache
sections.content:
**Neither LinkedHashMap nor HashMap+DLL is thread-safe**. Concurrent access causes data races, lost updates, or NPEs.

**Option 1: Wrap with synchronized block** (simple, low throughput):
```java
Map<Integer, Integer> lru = Collections.synchronizedMap(new LRUCache(capacity));
// Every op acquires one lock
```
**Problem**: serializes all access; scales poorly.

**Option 2: ReentrantReadWriteLock** (better, but reads and writes still contend):
```java
private final ReadWriteLock lock = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();
// Reads take read lock (shared)
// Writes take write lock (exclusive)
```
**Problem**: LRU's `get` is technically a write (moves entry), so read-write lock doesn't help much.

**Option 3: Caffeine (industry standard)**:
```java
LoadingCache<Integer, String> cache = Caffeine.newBuilder()
    .maximumSize(100)
    .expireAfterAccess(Duration.ofMinutes(10))
    .build(key -> loadFromDatabase(key));
```
- Uses lock-striping internally (like ConcurrentHashMap).
- Per-bucket locks; high throughput.
- TTL, expiry, statistics built-in.
- Recommended for production.

**Option 4: Google Guava's `LoadingCache`** — similar API, being superseded by Caffeine.

**Option 5: Custom concurrent LRU** — complex; use lock-striping on the HashMap and a concurrent linked list (CLHM). Hard to get right; don't reinvent.

**For interviews**: acknowledge that single-threaded LRU is the textbook problem; mention Caffeine/Guava for production concurrent use.

**Performance tips**:
- Caffeine: ~200ns per operation in low contention; ~500ns under contention. Close to in-memory HashMap.
- Avoid `Collections.synchronizedMap` for high-throughput systems.

sections.title: Variants — LFU, ARC, LRU with TTL
sections.content:
**LFU (Least Frequently Used)**: evict the entry accessed least often (tie-break: oldest among them).
- Implementation: frequency buckets (HashMap from count to doubly-linked list of nodes).
- Each node tracks its frequency; on access, move to the next-higher-count bucket.
- O(1) per op — tricky to implement correctly.
- Trade-off: LFU resists hot items eviction; LRU reacts faster to changing access patterns.

**LRU with TTL (Time To Live)**: entries expire after a fixed time.
- Add `expireAt` timestamp per entry.
- On `get`, check if expired; if so, treat as miss and evict.
- Optional: background thread or lazy expiry.
- Caffeine supports this natively.

**ARC (Adaptive Replacement Cache)**: balances LRU and LFU dynamically.
- Maintains two LRU queues: one for recently-used-once, one for recently-used-multiple-times.
- Adjusts sizes based on hit patterns.
- Used in production systems like ZFS.
- Complex to implement; third-party libraries.

**LRU-K**: considers K-th most recent access; harder to evict hot items.

**Clock algorithm**: approximation of LRU; uses a circular list with a reference bit. Lower overhead, used in OS page replacement.

**2Q**: two queues — FIFO for first-time accesses, LRU for repeat. Good resistance to scans.

**For interviews**: stick with LRU unless asked for a variant; mention ARC / LFU if pressed on 'when LRU isn't enough'.

sections.title: LinkedHashMap vs Manual HashMap+DLL
sections.content:
| Property | LinkedHashMap | HashMap + DLL |
|---|---|---|
| **Lines of code** | ~10 | ~40 |
| **Time per op** | O(1) | O(1) |
| **Space** | O(capacity) | O(capacity) |
| **Generic types** | Easy (inherit) | Manual |
| **Extensibility** | Limited (inheritance) | Full control |
| **Interview expectation** | 'You know this exists' | 'Implement it' |
| **Thread-safe** | No | No |
| **Null support** | Yes (one null key, null values) | Depends on impl |
| **Serializable** | Yes | Manual |
| **Used in production** | Yes, for simple caches | Yes, for custom caches |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **LRU cache**: fixed-capacity store with O(1) get and put; evicts least-recently-used.
- **Two implementations**: (1) LinkedHashMap with access order; (2) HashMap + doubly-linked list.
- **Must be O(1)**: HashMap for lookup + linked list for order.
- **Doubly-linked (not singly)**: needed for O(1) removal of arbitrary nodes.
- **Sentinel head/tail**: simplify code, eliminate null checks.
- **LinkedHashMap**: constructor flag `accessOrder = true`; override `removeEldestEntry`.
- **HashMap + DLL**: explicit, shows algorithm, easier to extend.
- **Not thread-safe**: use Caffeine, Guava, or `Collections.synchronizedMap` for concurrent.
- **Caffeine** is the industry standard: lock-striped, high throughput, TTL, stats.
- **Variants**: LFU (frequency-based), ARC (adaptive), TTL (expiry), 2Q, Clock.
- **Edge cases**: capacity 0 (always miss), capacity 1 (every put evicts), same key updates.
- **On get miss**: return -1, Optional.empty, or throw — API choice.
- **On put with existing key**: update value AND move to front.
- **On put when full**: evict LRU, then insert new (order matters: evict first to keep size stable).
- **Implementation details**: sentinel nodes, clean pointer updates, HashMap stores Node references.
- **Never forget to remove from HashMap when evicting** — common bug leading to memory leak.
- **For interviews**: implement HashMap + DLL; mention LinkedHashMap and Caffeine.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**LRU cache requirements**
- Fixed capacity
- O(1) get and put
- Evict least-recently-used when full
- Move to 'most recent' on access

**Why O(1)?**
- LRU is on hot paths (DB buffer, CDN, page cache)
- Any O(log n) or O(n) is unacceptable

**The data structures needed**

**HashMap for lookup**
- key → location in order structure
- O(1) access

**Linked list for order**
- Most recent at front
- Least recent at back
- Need O(1) insert at front, remove at back, move to front

**Why doubly-linked?**
- O(1) remove any node (need prev)
- Singly can't remove middle in O(1) (no prev pointer)
- Required for move-to-front in O(1)

**Sentinel head/tail nodes**
- Dummy nodes at both ends
- Eliminates null checks
- Internal nodes always have valid prev/next
- Cleaner code

**Two implementations**

**1. LinkedHashMap — short version**
- Extend LinkedHashMap
- Constructor: super(capacity, 0.75f, true) — accessOrder=true
- Override removeEldestEntry: return size() > capacity
- ~10 lines
- Uses JDK's built-in LinkedHashMap (HashMap + DLL under the hood)

**2. HashMap + DLL — interview version**
- Manual Node class with key, value, prev, next
- HashMap<Integer, Node>
- Sentinel head and tail nodes
- addToFront, removeNode, moveToFront helpers
- ~40 lines
- Shows understanding

**Get operation**
- Lookup key in HashMap → node
- If not found: return -1
- Move node to front (remove + addToFront)
- Return node.value

**Put operation**
- Lookup key in HashMap
- If exists: update value, move to front
- If not: check capacity
  - If full: evict tail.prev from both list and HashMap
  - Create new node, addToFront, put in HashMap

**Common bugs**

**1. Using singly-linked list**
- Can't O(1) remove middle
- Need doubly

**2. Using ArrayList**
- O(n) insert/delete
- Not O(1)

**3. Forgetting to update HashMap on eviction**
- Memory leak / stale key
- Always map.remove(evicted.key)

**4. Missing sentinel nodes**
- Null checks everywhere
- Bug-prone
- Always use sentinels

**5. Wrong order: update value vs move to front**
- Must do both on existing key

**6. Capacity 0 or 1**
- Capacity 0: everything misses
- Capacity 1: every put evicts
- Handle both gracefully

**Thread safety**

**Neither approach is thread-safe**
- Data races, lost updates, NPEs

**Options for concurrent**

**Collections.synchronizedMap**
- Single lock, serializes all access
- Low throughput

**ReentrantReadWriteLock**
- Limited help: LRU's get is effectively a write (moves entry)

**Caffeine (industry standard)**
- Lock-striped, like ConcurrentHashMap
- Per-bucket locks
- ~200ns per op in low contention
- TTL, expiry, stats built-in
- Use this in production

**Google Guava LoadingCache**
- Similar API
- Being superseded by Caffeine

**Variants**

**LFU (Least Frequently Used)**
- Frequency buckets
- More complex (O(1) each op)
- Resists eviction of hot items
- Slower to react to changes

**LRU with TTL**
- expireAt timestamp per entry
- On get: check if expired
- Caffeine native support

**ARC (Adaptive Replacement)**
- Balances LRU + LFU
- Two queues adjusted dynamically
- Used in ZFS
- Complex; use library

**Clock algorithm**
- Approximation of LRU
- Circular list with reference bit
- Low overhead
- OS page replacement

**2Q**
- FIFO for first-time + LRU for repeat
- Scan-resistant

**For interviews**
- Implement HashMap + DLL (shows algorithm)
- Mention LinkedHashMap as shortcut
- Discuss Caffeine for production concurrent use
- Address edge cases

**Recommendation:** For **interviews**, implement the **HashMap + doubly-linked list** approach — it demonstrates deep understanding of the O(1) invariants. Use **sentinel head/tail nodes** to eliminate null checks and keep the pointer operations clean. Always remember: **doubly-linked is required** for O(1) arbitrary-node removal; singly-linked forces O(n) to find predecessors. Mention **LinkedHashMap** as the idiomatic JDK shortcut — `new LinkedHashMap<>(capacity, 0.75f, true)` + `removeEldestEntry` gives you LRU in ~10 lines. For **production**, both manual and LinkedHashMap implementations are **not thread-safe**; use **Caffeine** (industry standard: lock-striped, ~200ns per op, supports TTL, stats, and async loading) or Guava's LoadingCache. Never use `Collections.synchronizedMap` for high-throughput scenarios — it serializes all access. Handle **edge cases**: capacity 0 (every get misses), capacity 1 (every put evicts), and duplicate-key puts (update value AND move to front). **Always remove from the HashMap when evicting** — a common bug leaves stale keys and leaks memory. Know the **variants** — **LFU** (frequency-based, harder to implement, resists hot-item eviction), **ARC** (adaptive, balances LRU and LFU), **TTL-based** caches (expiry on top of LRU), **Clock** (approximation used in OS page replacement). The mental model: **LRU = O(1) lookup (HashMap) + O(1) order maintenance (DLL)**. Once you've internalized the sentinel-node trick and the three pointer operations (addToFront, removeNode, moveToFront), the code writes itself.

followup_questions: Why must the list be doubly-linked and not singly-linked?
Why use sentinel head and tail nodes?
How would you make the LRU cache thread-safe for production?
What's the difference between LRU and LFU eviction policies?
How does Caffeine achieve high-throughput concurrent LRU?

questions.question: How do you check if two strings are anagrams in Java? Compare sort-and-compare vs frequency-counter approaches. Discuss complexity trade-offs and edge cases.
questions.title: Check if Two Strings Are Anagrams — Sort vs Frequency Counter in Java
questions.direct_answer: Two strings are **anagrams** if they contain the **same characters with the same frequencies**, just in different order (e.g., 'listen' and 'silent'). **Two main approaches**: (1) **Sort both and compare**: `Arrays.sort(a.toCharArray())` + `Arrays.sort(b.toCharArray())` and compare. Time **O(n log n)** (sorting), space **O(n)** (char array copy). (2) **Frequency counter**: count char occurrences in `a`, decrement for `b`; if all counts end at 0, they're anagrams. Time **O(n)**, space **O(Σ)** where Σ is alphabet size. **For ASCII** (common case), use `int[26]` (lowercase) or `int[128]` — O(1) space effectively. **For Unicode**, use `HashMap<Character, Integer>`. **Frequency counter is the canonical interview answer**: linear time, constant space, works for any alphabet. **First check length**: if `a.length() != b.length()`, immediately return false. **Edge cases**: empty strings (anagrams by definition — but depends on spec), case sensitivity (decide: 'Listen' and 'Silent' are anagrams if case-insensitive), non-letter characters (spaces, punctuation — strip or keep depending on context), Unicode (surrogates need careful handling). **Variants**: **Find all anagrams of pattern in string** (sliding window + frequency), **Group anagrams** (use sorted-string or frequency-tuple as key in HashMap), **Valid anagram check for a stream of chars** (maintain running frequency). **Compare with isomorphic strings**: isomorphic means 1:1 mapping of characters; different constraint. **For production**, pre-normalize (lowercase, strip whitespace) based on spec. Frequency counter with `int[26]` is the **simplest, fastest, and most interview-friendly** version for ASCII input.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows both approaches, can compare complexity, handle length check early, and address edge cases (case sensitivity, Unicode, whitespace)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not checking lengths first. Using sort when frequency would be O(n). Ignoring case sensitivity spec. Mishandling Unicode with char[] (surrogates)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the int[26] optimization for lowercase ASCII, mention Unicode surrogate-pair handling, extend to group-anagrams and find-all-anagrams problems, address normalization (case, whitespace, diacritics)

sections.title: Frequency Counter — O(n) Time, O(1) Space for ASCII
Sort-and-Compare — O(n log n) Time
Variants — Group Anagrams, Find Anagrams in String
Edge Cases and Normalization
Sort vs Frequency Counter — Side by Side
sections.content:
| Property | Sort-and-Compare | Frequency Counter |
|---|---|---|
| **Time** | O(n log n) | O(n) |
| **Space** | O(n) (char[] copies) | O(1) for fixed alphabet, O(Σ) for HashMap |
| **Simplicity** | 4 lines | ~6 lines |
| **Unicode** | Works naturally | Need HashMap for non-ASCII |
| **Performance for long strings** | Slower (log factor) | Faster (linear) |
| **Performance for short strings** | Similar | Slightly faster |
| **Interview preference** | OK, simpler | Preferred, linear |
| **Extensibility (variants)** | For group-anagrams: use sorted key | For group-anagrams: use frequency-tuple key |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Anagram**: same characters, same frequencies, any order.
- **Frequency counter** (preferred): O(n) time, O(Σ) space; for ASCII, O(1) with int[26].
- **Sort-and-compare**: O(n log n) time, O(n) space; simpler but slower.
- **Always check lengths first**: if different, not anagrams.
- **Increment for s, decrement for t**: if all zero, anagram.
- **int[26]** for lowercase letters; **int[128]** for ASCII; **HashMap** for Unicode.
- **Surrogate pairs**: iterate via `codePoints()` for emoji and rare characters.
- **Normalization**: lowercase, strip whitespace / punctuation / diacritics based on spec.
- **Edge cases**: empty strings (trivially anagrams), one empty, single char, case, Unicode.
- **Variants**: group anagrams (sorted string or frequency tuple as key), find all anagrams in string (sliding window + frequency match).
- **Group anagrams key**: sorted string is O(k log k); frequency tuple is O(k).
- **Find all anagrams**: sliding window of size |p|; Arrays.equals on int[26] is O(1).
- **Null handling**: decide and document behavior (throw vs false).
- **For interviews**: recommend frequency counter with int[26]; mention sort as alternative; address Unicode and normalization.
- **Compare to isomorphic strings**: isomorphic is 1:1 character mapping (different constraint).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Two main approaches**

**1. Frequency counter (preferred)**
- Check lengths first; if different, false
- Array int[26] for lowercase ASCII (or int[128])
- For each char in s: increment; for each in t: decrement
- If all counts zero at end: anagram
- **Time O(n), Space O(1)** for ASCII

**2. Sort and compare**
- Sort both char arrays, compare
- Simpler, but **O(n log n) time, O(n) space**
- Acceptable for short strings

**Always start with length check**
- O(1) shortcut
- If lengths differ, return false immediately

**Alphabet choices**

**ASCII lowercase**
- int[26]
- s.charAt(i) - 'a'
- O(1) space
- Fastest

**Full ASCII**
- int[128]
- s.charAt(i) as index
- O(1) space

**Unicode**
- HashMap<Character, Integer>
- O(Σ) space (distinct chars)
- Slower due to hashing

**Surrogate pairs (emoji)**
- s.length() counts char units, not code points
- Iterate via s.codePoints() for full Unicode support
- Rare in interviews but real in production

**Normalization (production)**
- Case sensitivity: `.toLowerCase()` if ignoring case
- Whitespace: `.replaceAll("\\s+", "")` if ignoring spaces
- Punctuation: `.replaceAll("\\p{Punct}", "")`
- Diacritics: Normalizer.NFD + strip marks
- Decide based on spec

**Edge cases**

**Empty strings**
- "" and "": trivially anagrams (spec-dependent)
- "" and "a": length differs, false

**Single character**
- "a" and "a": true
- "a" and "b": false

**Case sensitivity**
- 'Listen' and 'Silent': case-sensitive false, case-insensitive true
- Clarify with interviewer

**Whitespace**
- 'a b c' and 'c b a': false if whitespace matters
- Typical anagram problems ignore whitespace

**Null**
- Throw or return false; decide and document

**Variants**

**Group anagrams**
- Given array of strings, group anagrams together
- Key: sorted string (O(k log k)) or frequency tuple (O(k))
- Frequency tuple is faster for long strings
- Store in HashMap<String, List<String>>

**Find all anagrams of p in s**
- Sliding window of size |p|
- Maintain frequency array
- Arrays.equals on int[26] is O(1) — effectively O(n) total

**Valid anagram with frequencies**
- Two multisets equal
- Same technique

**Isomorphic strings (different concept)**
- Characters map 1:1
- 'egg' and 'add' are isomorphic, not anagrams
- Different constraint

**Common pitfalls**

**1. Not checking lengths first**
- Unnecessary O(n) work

**2. Using sort when frequency is O(n)**
- Sort is O(n log n) — worse for long strings

**3. Assuming ASCII when input is Unicode**
- int[26] fails for non-letter
- Use HashMap

**4. Surrogate pair bugs**
- Emoji / rare chars use two char units
- Use codePoints() for safety

**5. Ignoring case when required**
- Clarify with interviewer
- Add .toLowerCase() if case-insensitive

**6. Not handling whitespace / punctuation**
- Normalize first in production

**For interviews**
- Recommend **frequency counter with int[26]**
- Start with length check
- Mention sort as simpler alternative
- Address Unicode if input is general
- Extend to group-anagrams if asked

**Recommendation:** For **checking if two strings are anagrams**, the **frequency counter** approach is the canonical interview answer — O(n) time, O(1) space for ASCII (with int[26]), linear and cache-friendly. Always **start with a length check** (O(1) shortcut for mismatches). Use **int[26]** for lowercase letters, **int[128]** for full ASCII, or a **HashMap<Character, Integer>** for Unicode. For **surrogate pairs** (emoji, rare characters), iterate via `codePoints()` since `char` is 16-bit and can't hold all code points. Mention the **sort-and-compare** approach as simpler (4 lines) but O(n log n) and O(n) space — slower for long strings. For **variants**: **group anagrams** uses either a sorted string or a frequency tuple as a HashMap key; the frequency tuple is O(k) per key, faster for long strings. **Find all anagrams of a pattern in a string** uses a sliding window of size |p| with frequency matching. Always **normalize according to spec**: lowercase, strip whitespace, punctuation, and diacritics depending on the problem definition. Know the difference from **isomorphic strings** (1:1 character mapping, different constraint). The mental model: **anagram check = equal frequency distributions**; frequency counter makes this O(n) linear; length check is the cheap first gate. Once you've internalized the int[26] pattern, many string-frequency problems use the same template.
